title: Security Without Humans: Designing Systems That Defend Themselves
takeaways: From visibility to autonomous resilience—with Intent, Time, and Interaction as structural guardrails for machine-speed cyber defense.
RSA Conference Official Library companion presentation by Harsh Verma, Principal Software Engineer - AI.

title: Visibility Is Not Resilience: Moving Beyond Alert-Centric Security
takeaways: Contrasts today's alert-centric pipeline (Telemetry -> Alert -> Queue -> Analyst decision) constrained by escalation latency against autonomous resilience (Telemetry -> Context + Policy -> Bounded action -> Verified recovery).
Core design goal: remove repetitive delay—not human accountability—allowing routine, reversible threats to be contained at machine speed inside explicit policy boundaries.

title: The Response Loop Is Being Outpaced
takeaways: Traces autonomous attack progression across Signal (anomalous behavior), Decision (context evaluation), Delegation (tool or peer agent invocation), and Impact (data, identity, or workflow changes).
Explains why a human approval loop at every step becomes a bottleneck—especially for low-risk, repeatable containment.

title: Security Is a Property of the Whole System: Intent, Time, and Interaction
takeaways: Frames autonomous-system security across three interacting dimensions: Intent (does the action match the approved objective?), Time (how does risk change as context and state evolve?), and Interaction (how can trust and privilege propagate between actors?).
No single control can guarantee safety when the system continuously changes through delegation and autonomous action.

title: Threat Path: How Compromises Travel Through Trusted Workflows
takeaways: Maps the 4-stage propagation chain: 01 Untrusted Input -> 02 Agent Misreads content as authority -> 03 Trust Propagates to peer agents/tools -> 04 Workflow Impact across data, identity, and operations.
Highlights the core defensive question: where can the execution chain be interrupted before trust becomes transitive?

title: Closing the Loop: The 6-Stage Self-Defending System Lifecycle
takeaways: Defines the closed-loop autonomous response sequence: 1 Sense -> 2 Assess (identity, intent, risk) -> 3 Contain (smallest reversible action) -> 4 Restore (trusted state) -> 5 Verify (controls and service health) -> 6 Learn (update policies and detections).
Enforces a strict Policy Gate: every autonomous action must be explainable, scoped, logged, and reversible where possible.

title: A Reference Architecture for Autonomous Defense
takeaways: Connects Protected Environments (Agents & Copilots, Apps & APIs, Cloud & Endpoints) to an Autonomous Defense Plane organized across Observe -> Decide -> Enforce -> Recover.
Spans continuous Governance across every layer via risk appetite tiers, policy ownership & exceptions, immutable audit trails, and human escalation & override.

title: Guardrail 01 — Intent: Bind Every Action to an Approved Purpose
takeaways: Identity alone answers who; Intent answers why an actor is acting and what it is allowed to accomplish via an explicit Intent Contract (Purpose, Actor, Resource, Allowed Action, Data Scope, Expiry).
Illustrates point-of-action authorization: read-only invoice metadata matches approved intent (ALLOW), while changing payment destination or releasing funds violates scope (DENY / ESCALATE).

title: Guardrail 02 — Time: Trust Has a Half-Life
takeaways: Addresses permissions that were safe at task start becoming unsafe after state changes, anomalies, or context shifts across Issue -> Re-Evaluate -> Expire -> Revoke / Renew.
Establishes three temporal controls: Short Leases (reduce stale authority), Event-Driven Checks (reassess after drift), and Safe Expiry (fail closed for sensitive actions).

title: Guardrail 03 — Interaction: Stop Trust from Becoming Contagious
takeaways: Models multi-hop delegation graphs (User -> Orchestrator -> Data Agent / Payment Agent -> Resource) protected by per-hop authorization, provenance, and scope preservation.
Enforces non-transitive trust by default: permission to call one agent does not imply permission to use every capability reachable through it.

title: Adaptive Defense Framework: Five Building Blocks of Continuous Control
takeaways: Details the five continuous building blocks: 01 Behavioral Monitoring -> 02 Policy Enforcement -> 03 Contextual Trust -> 04 Autonomous Remediation -> 05 Self-Adjusting Controls.
Reinforces that adaptive defense does not mean unconstrained: every policy update must be tested, explainable, and reversible.

title: Governance by Design: The L0–L3 Autonomy Risk Envelope
takeaways: Defines a four-tier operating envelope: L0 Observe (collect evidence), L1 Recommend (human review), L2 Bounded Auto (preapproved reversible containment), and L3 Approval Required (high-impact or irreversible actions).
Core operating rule: default to the narrowest authority that can safely achieve the defensive objective.

title: Illustrative Scenario Walkthrough: Containing a Compromised Workflow
takeaways: Walks through an untrusted invoice attachment prompt-injection attack path countered at each stage by Intent (read-only scope), Time (short-lived token), Interaction (per-hop auth denying privilege inheritance), and Recovery (quarantine document, revoke session, verify state).
Demonstrates containing the workflow before payment state mutation while preserving forensic evidence for review.

title: Industry Applications: Same Resilience Pattern Across Critical Sectors
takeaways: Applies bounded autonomous resilience across Financial Services (hold suspicious transfer, revoke session), Healthcare (isolate compromised integration while preserving clinical availability), Manufacturing/OT (segment gateway), and Cloud & SaaS (revoke token, restore config).
Synthesizes the cross-sector pattern: detect context -> choose smallest safe action -> verify service health -> recover.

title: Operating Metrics: Measure Resilience, Not Just Alert Volume
takeaways: Measures speed, scope, and recovery quality via MTTD (Mean Time to Detect), MTTC (Mean Time to Contain), MTTR (Mean Time to Recover), and Blast Radius (affected assets/users).
Tracks automation safety metrics: false-containment rate, successful rollback/restore rate, policy override and escalation rate, and audit-evidenced action coverage.

title: Human Governance: How Autonomy Changes the Work Humans Do
takeaways: Separates organizational duties across Humans Define (risk appetite, approved action tiers, policy ownership), Systems Execute (evidence collection, low-risk containment, token revocation), and Humans Review (high-consequence actions, ambiguous intent, post-incident learning).
Establishes the governing principle: delegate execution—never delegate accountability.

title: Implementation Roadmap: A Practical 90-Day Path to Bounded Autonomy
takeaways: Outlines a three-phase rollout: Days 0–30 Baseline (map agents, identities, rollback paths), Days 31–60 Shadow + Simulate (observe-only mode and incident replay), and Days 61–90 Bounded Autonomy (enable low-risk reversible actions for one workflow).
Mandates disciplined scaling: never scale autonomy faster than you can measure, audit, and reverse it.

title: Design Checklist: Seven Principles for Systems That Defend Themselves
takeaways: Architecture review checklist: 01 Least privilege by default, 02 Authorization bound to intent, 03 Short-lived scoped delegation, 04 Continuous trust re-evaluation, 05 Smallest safe containment action, 06 Verified recovery, 07 Retained human accountability.
A system is not self-defending because it can act—it is self-defending when it can act safely, prove what happened, and recover.

title: The Next Security Model: Machine-Speed Defense Within Human Boundaries
takeaways: Don't remove humans from responsibility—remove humans from repetitive delay.
Build systems that can defend, recover, and explain—at machine speed, within human-defined boundaries.

title: References & Further Reading: Primary Source + Foundational Standards
takeaways: Cites the primary RSA Conference Blog article ('Security Without Humans: Designing Systems that Defend Themselves', Nov 13, 2026) as the source for the Intent, Time, and Interaction framing.
Grounds architecture guidance in NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture), NIST AI RMF 1.0, NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (Incident Response), and MITRE ATLAS.

title: References & Further Reading: Security Practice + Industry Frameworks
takeaways: Connects OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 (excessive agency and prompt injection) and CISA Secure by Design principles to autonomous cyber defense.
References industry initiatives including DARPA AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC) and autonomous security copilot patterns.
